LINE constructs its language network by treating words as nodes and connecting two words with an edge when they co-occur within a fixed context window in the text. The edge weight is typically the number of times the pair appears together, so the resulting graph is a weighted word co-occurrence network. LINE then learns low-dimensional embeddings from this graph by preserving first-order proximity (direct edge weights) and second-order proximity (similar neighborhood/context distributions).

DBLP citation data is ideal for word co-occurrence modeling because it is naturally sparse, large-scale, and highly skewed, with many meaningful pairwise relationships but far fewer than in a dense graph. That matches the assumptions of word co-occurrence networks, where only a small fraction of all possible word pairs actually co-occur. In addition, citation-style data and text co-occurrence graphs both exhibit strong local association structure and heavy-tailed degree distributions, making them well suited for LINE’s scalable embedding objective.
